q: Does re-fitting the generalized k+m stage MVK model (Little-Wright 2003) to modern SEER colon-cancer incidence (1973-2020, ~50 years now vs the paper's 1973-2002 window) still yield the paper's claimed ordering: 2-stage Nowak and 2-stage Little-Wright co-tied for best, 4-stage Luebeck-Moolgavkar acceptable, and 5-stage significantly worse (P<0.01)? Or has the additional 18 years of follow-up, plus improved screening-driven early detection, changed which stage-count is preferred?
basis: REPORT.md claim C6 is DATA-BLOCKED because the SEER microdata is SEER*Stat-registration gated and the Little-Wright k+m-stage Poisson-likelihood fitter has never been publicly released. The paper's headline model-comparison claim rests entirely on this fit, which no external audit has ever reproduced. Modern SEER data is now much larger and screening-corrected.
next_steps: 1) Register for a free SEER*Stat account and pull SEER18 colon-adenocarcinoma incidence by sex, single-year age, single-year calendar year, 1973-2020. 2) Re-implement the Little-Wright generalized k+m stage MVK Poisson likelihood from Math Biosci 183:111 equations (roughly 200 lines of Python + scipy.optimize). 3) Fit k in {2,3,4,5} x m in {0,1,2} on the microdata; compare log-likelihoods and Akaike weights. 4) Report whether the paper's ordering (2-stage best; 5-stage significantly worse) still holds, or whether extended follow-up + screening-era heterogeneity has shifted the ranking. Free-endpoint eligible.

q: How sensitive is the Schollnberger SVM bystander-protection U-shape to the competing-risk formulation choice? Specifically, if the constant-hazard cell-death removal in the SVM is replaced with an age-dependent hazard (Gompertz-like for cell senescence), does the delayed-vs-immediate plating ordering of k_ap survive, or does the U-shape flatten / invert at low doses?
basis: The paper (Talk 4) and REPORT.md claim C4 both treat the SVM's cell-death removal term as effectively constant-rate. The bystander apoptosis term k_ap enters multiplicatively with a fixed dose-saturating factor. Whether the U-shape is a genuine dose-response feature or an artifact of the constant-hazard assumption has never been probed in the LUCID audit (only the qualitative U-shape was reproduced).
next_steps: 1) In the existing code/smoke_replication.py SVM stub, replace the constant cell-death rate with a two-parameter Gompertz form h_death(t) = h0 * exp(g*t). 2) Sweep g over [0, 0.005, 0.02, 0.05] per day and re-plot the dose-response at D in {0, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500} mGy. 3) Measure the depth of the low-dose dip vs g and check whether the delayed>immediate k_ap ordering (0.054 vs 0.022 per day) is preserved across g values. 4) If the U-shape vanishes for g>0.02/d, that would substantially weaken the paper's protective-bystander headline. Pure analytic, no external data, free-endpoint eligible.

q: Extending to low-dose radon and diagnostic-CT ranges (1-100 mSv), do the two-stage MVK / TSCE hazard predictions from the paper's Talks 1-3 agree quantitatively with modern epidemiological benchmarks (BEIR-VII 2006, UNSCEAR 2020, ICRP 103)? The paper never tabulates its ERR/EAR predictions against these standards.
basis: REPORT.md and the paper both stop at qualitative claims about the MVK hazard shape (monotone rise across adult ages). Neither provides an ERR/EAR table comparable to BEIR-VII's tables 12D-1 through 12D-3 or UNSCEAR 2020 Annex B. The gap between mechanistic-model prediction and consensus-committee empirical fit is one of the most operationally important questions in low-dose radiation protection.
next_steps: 1) Using the code/claim_audit.py MVK plateau formula, compute predicted lifetime attributable risk (LAR) per Sievert for solid cancers at age-at-exposure {10, 30, 50, 70} for both sexes, assuming a chronic 100 mSv exposure. 2) Compare to BEIR-VII Table 12D-1 (all solid cancers) and UNSCEAR 2020 Annex B site-specific tables. 3) Report percent deviation and identify which age-at-exposure bins the mechanistic model over- or under-predicts. 4) If deviations exceed a factor of 2, flag the MVK-family model as insufficient at diagnostic-dose ranges. BEIR-VII and UNSCEAR tables are free-download PDFs; MVK code already exists in the slot. Free-endpoint eligible.

q: How does the paper's TSCE-based individual-heterogeneity claim for Thorotrast liver cancer (claim C8: at least 95 percent of the population at age 40 has baseline risk under 10 percent of the mean; top percentile over 10x the mean) compare to modern polygenic-risk-score (PRS) distributions from GWAS-informed liver-cancer models? Does the mechanistic-parameter heterogeneity assumed by TSCE approximately match, exceed, or under-shoot the empirical PRS spread?
basis: Claim C8 is DATA-BLOCKED because the Heidenreich-Luebeck-Hazelton 2002 fitted posterior parameter set was never released. But modern liver-cancer PRS distributions (e.g. from UK Biobank hepatocellular-carcinoma GWAS) are published as summary statistics. Comparing the two heterogeneity distributions is a novel cross-check the paper could not do in 2007 but is straightforward now.
next_steps: 1) Pull published UK Biobank HCC GWAS summary statistics (open-access via GWAS Catalog) and compute the population distribution of log-relative-risk under a standard PRS construction. 2) Compare the resulting inter-individual spread (interquartile range, top-percentile ratio) to the paper's claim of 95 percent under 10 percent of mean and top percentile over 10x mean. 3) If PRS spread is markedly narrower than TSCE-implied heterogeneity, that suggests the TSCE fit is absorbing unmodeled environmental variance into apparent genetic heterogeneity. Report the ratio explicitly. All inputs are open-access GWAS summary stats. Free-endpoint eligible.

q: Does an ML-driven meta-model (e.g. gradient-boosted tree or shallow neural net) trained on multi-cohort radiation epidemiology data (LSS, INWORKS, Techa River, Mayak) outperform the paper's mechanistic MVK/TSCE family in cross-cohort risk prediction? And if so, does it recover the same age-at-exposure and time-since-exposure patterns that MVK predicts mechanistically, or does it identify additional structure that the biological model misses?
basis: The paper (2008) explicitly limits itself to mechanistic biological models and does not consider data-driven alternatives. The last 5 years of low-dose radiation epidemiology have seen INWORKS 2015 and 2023 updates plus Techa River / Mayak follow-ups that were not available to the paper's authors. A modern ML vs mechanistic comparison would establish whether the mechanistic constraint helps or hurts predictive accuracy.
next_steps: 1) Assemble published-summary-level ERR-per-Gy estimates from LSS (Preston 2007 + Grant 2017 updates), INWORKS (Richardson 2015 + 2023), Techa River (Krestinina), and Mayak (Sokolnikov) cohorts (all published in tables in open-access papers). 2) Fit a leave-one-cohort-out cross-validated gradient-boosted regressor on age-at-exposure, sex, time-since-exposure, dose. 3) Compare cross-cohort predictive RMSE against the MVK/TSCE closed-form predictions from code/smoke_replication.py. 4) Inspect SHAP values to see whether the ML model recovers the two-stage MVK age dependence or identifies unmodeled interaction terms. All data is published tables; no microdata required. Free-endpoint eligible.
